content.intro: Code Quality and Style is lesson 163 in Testing, Code Quality, and Maintainability. Tests make intended behavior executable. Unit tests target small logic; integration tests verify that real components cooperate across a boundary.
content.why_it_matters: Tests provide fast feedback about behavior; a green test suite is evidence, not a proof of every property. This lesson focuses on code quality and style and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Tests make intended behavior executable. Unit tests target small logic; integration tests verify that real components cooperate across a boundary.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for code quality and style. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Naming conventions
items.text: Identifiers must follow lexical rules and avoid reserved keywords unless escaped. Prefer consistent C# naming conventions so readers can recognize types, members, locals, and constants quickly.

items.title: Formatting and indentation
items.text: For formatting and indentation, define the expected behavior, inspect how it relates to code quality and style, and verify a representative case plus one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Analyzer diagnostics
items.text: Create a reproducible case, inspect the state at the failure boundary, and log structured context that helps diagnosis.

items.title: Compiler warnings
items.text: Separate source diagnostics, emitted assembly artifacts, and runtime execution; they are different stages with different failure modes.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates code quality and style. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates code quality and style rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for code quality and style before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
